The knifejaw Oplegnathus woodwardi is a temperate reef fish endemic to the waters surrounding southern Australia, where it occupies shallow rocky habitats with abundant encrusting invertebrate prey. Early life stages of this species are pelagic, with fertilised eggs hatching into yolk-sac larvae that undergo a brief endotrophic phase before commencing first exogenous feeding. At a water temperature of 14.8 °C [T = 14.8 °C], the interval from fertilisation to eclosion lasts 11.8 days [ab = 11.8 days], a developmental period that aligns closely with that of other temperate spariform fishes with similarly sized eggs. The newly emerged prolarvae carry a substantial yolk reserve, and their mass at the moment of hatching is approximately 0.00027 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00027 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of 0.8 millimeters observed in captive spawning studies. Following the transition to exogenous nutrition, these larvae progress through flexion and postflexion stages before undergoing a dramatic metamorphic climax associated with settlement into the benthic habitat, where they take on the characteristic adult morphology.

As individuals transition into the post-settlement juvenile phase, growth proceeds rapidly during the first several years of life, with body length increasing at a rate that gradually decelerates as the fish approach their asymptotic size. Mark-recapture studies and otolith-based ageing have provided robust estimates of the ultimate standard length attained by this species, which reaches 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters] in the local population, a value consistent with the maximum lengths reported for Oplegnathus woodwardi in museum records. The corresponding maximum wet weight for an individual of this ultimate length is approximately 1890 grams [Wwi = approximately 1890 grams], a figure obtained from length-weight regressions fitted to a large sample of specimens collected across the species' geographic range. This substantial adult body mass places the knifejaw among the larger members of its genus, although individuals from more northerly populations tend to achieve slightly smaller maximum dimensions, possibly reflecting latitudinal gradients in productivity or temperature.

Sexual maturation in Oplegnathus woodwardi occurs after several years of somatic growth, with the onset of gonadal activity linked to both age and body size thresholds. The standard length at which 50 percent of individuals are estimated to have reached puberty is 27.7 centimeters [Lp = 27.7 centimeters], a value derived from histological examination of gonadal tissue in a size-structured sample collected over multiple spawning seasons. At this length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 438 grams [Wwp = approximately 438 grams], a mass that appears to reflect the accumulation of sufficient somatic reserves to support the energetic demands of gametogenesis and spawning activity. The age at which this pubertal length is typically attained, based on growth models fitted to tag-recapture data, is approximately six years, indicating that knifejaws adopt a relatively slow, late-maturing life history strategy compared to many other temperate labrids and sparids that reproduce at younger ages.

Reproductive allocation in female knifejaw has been quantified through detailed histological and gravimetric analysis of ovaries collected during the peak spawning period. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged 6% [GSI = 6%] under the typical thermal conditions of the austral summer spawning season at 14.8 °C [T = 14.8 °C]. This relatively modest investment in ovarian tissue relative to body mass is characteristic of iteroparous marine fishes that spawn repeatedly over a protracted breeding season, rather than releasing a single large batch of eggs. The spawning period itself extends from late winter through early summer, with individual females likely capable of multiple spawning bouts separated by intervals of oocyte recruitment and vitellogenesis, a pattern that distributes reproductive effort across several months and buffers annual reproductive success against interannual fluctuations in oceanographic conditions.

Comprehensive life history data indicate that Oplegnathus woodwardi is a relatively long-lived species, with the maximum documented lifespan in the wild estimated at 50 years [am = 50 years] when maintained at an average annual water temperature of 14.8 °C [T = 14.8 °C], a value inferred from edge-counts of sectioned otoliths from the oldest individuals in the population. This extreme longevity, uncommon among temperate fishes of its body size, is coupled with a late age at maturity and moderate annual fecundity, producing a life history syndrome that is highly sensitive to changes in adult mortality rates imposed by fishing pressure. Population modelling has demonstrated that the combination of such a long lifespan (50 years) [am = 50 years] and delayed maturation renders the species particularly vulnerable to overexploitation, as the removal of large, old individuals disproportionately diminishes the reproductive potential of the stock and slows the capacity for population recovery following disturbance at a temperature of 14.8 °C [T = 14.8 °C].
